title: Procedure
content:
1. Clean the plano-convex lens and the glass plate thoroughly, then place the lens with its curved surface facing down onto the plate, and mount the assembly in the apparatus holder.

2. Switch on the sodium vapour lamp and allow it a few minutes to stabilize and reach full brightness.

3. Adjust the 45° glass plate above the lens-plate assembly so that light from the lamp is reflected straight down onto it, illuminating the setup uniformly.

4. Focus the travelling microscope on the ring system from above until sharp, well-defined concentric rings are visible, with the central dark spot exactly at the intersection of the eyepiece crosswires.

5. Determine the least count of the microscope: note the value of one main scale division (M) and the total number of vernier divisions (N), then compute LC = M/N.

6. Move the microscope to one side of the pattern (for example, to the 20th dark ring) and record the main scale reading (MSR) and vernier scale reading (VSR) when the crosswire is exactly tangential to that ring; compute the total reading R1.

7. Continuing to move in the same direction (never reversing, to avoid backlash error), pass across the center and take the corresponding reading on the opposite side of the same ring; compute R2.

8. Repeat steps 6-7 for rings 16, 12, 8, and 4 (or as specified by your instructor), always continuing the microscope's motion in one direction only.

9. Tabulate MSR, VSR, and Total Reading for both sides of each ring, then compute D = |R1 − R2| and D² for every ring measured.

10. Pair up rows with a fixed interval m (commonly 4) — for example rings 20 & 16, 16 & 12, 12 & 8, 8 & 4 — and compute D²(n+m) − D²(n) for each pair; take the mean of these differences.

11. Determine R, the radius of curvature of the lens, using a spherometer if it hasn't already been supplied.

12. Calculate λ1 using the mean difference in the algebraic formula.

13. Plot a graph of D² (y-axis) against ring number (x-axis); it should form a straight line. Determine its slope using two well-separated points on the best-fit line, then calculate λ2 = slope / (4R).

14. Average λ1 and λ2 to get the final experimental wavelength, and compute the percentage error against the standard value (5893 Å).
